newsitem.title: UK: Yeltsin could be sicker than admitted, experts say.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin could be sicker than admitted, experts say.

text.p: Although Russian President Boris Yeltsin has officially been admitted to hospital with pneumonia, he could well be sicker than the Kremlin is willing to concede, Western doctors said on Thursday.
Russian officials said Yeltsin, who had major heart bypass surgery two months ago, was being treated with antibiotics and was still fit to run the country.

But international heart experts said it was possible that Yeltsin -- who looked frail during a meeting last week with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl -- had suffered some sort of heart failure which had triggered pneumonia-like symptoms.

"It seems likely that what he's got is a mixture of a chest infection and heart failure. He really looked a very sick man," said Professor Brian Pentecost, medical director of the British Heart Foundation.

"It's disappointing he should be in this position so soon after surgery...I wouldn't think we'd see him bouncing again like he was last year," he said, referring to Yeltsin's exertions before winning the Russian presidential election.
In Moscow, Russian heart surgeon Renat Akchurin, who led the team which operated on Yeltsin last November, said the president's doctors had told him he was in "a quite satisfactory" condition.
Akchurin told reporters the pneumonia was not related to the operation and that the president's overall health allowed him to perform his duties.
Pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey who advised Akchurin over Yeltsin's heart surgery, joined his Russian colleagues in ruling out a link with the operation.
Asked if Yeltsin had recovered from the trauma of the heart surgery, DeBakey said: "I would say pretty much yes and his heart is functioning now virtually normally."

Pentecost said even if Yeltsin were suffering just from pneumonia there was reason to be worried about his health, especially in view of reports that he had scarred heart tissue which could have drastically reduced the effectiveness of the bypasses.
"One of main problems of pneumonia is that it causes the oxygen content of the blood to fall," Pentecost said.
"The combined effect of scarred heart muscles and low oxygen can throw the patient into heart failure. This is a life-threatening condition," he added.
German heart surgeon Professor Hermann Sons, head of the cardiological centre in Kassel, told Reuters that Yeltsin needed plenty of rest.
"I would keep him in hospital or in a sanatorium -- anyway, under doctors' control -- for four weeks," he said.
But Dr Fikrat Shabbo, a heart surgeon at Guy's Hospital in London, said it was clear Yeltsin had not had enough time to recover from surgery before going back to work.

"It takes a normal heart surgery patient about three months to recover and he hasn't had three months. A guy running a big country is probably never left alone and therefore it takes longer to return to normal," he said.
Shabbo said the Russian leader could have suffered some sort of heart failure which had caused fluid to build up in his lungs and then become infected.

"We see this sometimes after heart surgery and this kind of infection is more dangerous than a simple problem with the lungs because of the heart failure. It all depends on how early you catch it," he said.
Yeltsin had five heart bypasses in early November to overcome blood supply problems and some experts said it was possible that one of the grafts had collapsed.
"One must wonder whether he'll be able to continue with the burdens of office," said Pentecost.
"The likelihood is that it does appear his ability to undertake physical activity will gradually diminish and he will find the strains of being a head of state all too much."

The experts ruled out the idea of a heart transplant, saying Yeltsin's weakened condition -- he also has some kidney damage -- meant the 65-year-old Russian leader could die if subjected to such surgery..

"The problem is that, as we get into our mid-60s, so many of our other functions begin to deteriorate and our ability to ride out the stresses and strains of transplants are greatly diminished," said Pentecost.
